images.caption:
A 22-unit condominium located at 2001 19th Street, N.W. – also known as 1866 California Street, N.W. – in the Adams Morgan neighborhood of Washington, D.C.
Built in 1908 (land–$17,000; construction–$63,000) to the designs of architect Waddy B. Wood, the 42-room, Tudor Revival-style building originally served as the Office of the Qing Legation, and later as the Embassy of the Republic of China.

The building is designated as a contributing property to the Washington Heights Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2006.

images.caption:
The Belmont Lofts (known as the Belmont Arts Building until 2001) located at 1800 Belmont Road, NW in the Adams Morgan neighborhood of Washington, D.C. Designed by local architect George S. Cooper in 1900, the Queen Anne building is a contributing property to the Washington Heights Historic District. 
Notable past tenants include author Mírzá Aḥmad Sohráb and John H. Edwards, an Assistant Secretary of the Treasury. The first floor retail space (2322 18th Street, NW) is currently leased to a MaggieMoo's franchise. The remaining floors serve as residential units.

images.caption: Late 19th-century homes, located at 2433–2443 18th Street, N.W., in the Adams Morgan neighborhood of Washington, D.C.  Built in 1897 for developer John Sherman, 2433–2443 were designed by noted architect Waddy B. Wood, all but one in the Italianate and Queen Anne architectural styles.  Converted to commercial use in the 1920s, the shops and restaurants are designated as contributing properties to the Washington Heights Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2006.  From 1956 to 1962, pioneering gay rights activist Frank Kameny lived in a top-floor apartment at 2435 18th Street, N.W., the dark brown building visible on the right-hand side.

images.caption:
2473–2477 18th Street, N.W., (right to left) in the Adams Morgan neighborhood of Washington, D.C.
Built as a single dwelling in 1902, the brick, Queen Anne residence was designed by architect Nicholas R. Grimm for developer Harry Wardman.   The row house – now converted into three commercial units, but still listed under one owner – is designated as a contributing property to the Washington Heights Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2006.

The store fronts pictured are Saki Asian Grille (left), CD/Game Exchange (center; closed), and Caliyogurt (right).
